criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community drinking-water service access across core urban and peri-urban wards in two municipalities of Nepal (Tansen and Damauli).
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study analyses the legal, institutional, and governance performance of community-managed Drinking Water Users' Associations (DWUAs) and water cooperatives under Nepal's Water Resource Act 1992, Drinking Water Regulation 1998, and Local Self Governance Act 1999. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, while much of the narrative addresses general WUA management, source maintenance, and corruption in pump repairs, the paper also empirically examines specific rule-type mechanisms directly governing household service access: (1) utility ownership and regulatory structure (autonomous statutory DWUAs/cooperatives operating under their own constitutions independently of municipal regulatory scrutiny); (2) tariff and connection-charge rules without pro-poor subsidies (NPR 50,000 / USD 440 upfront fee for a new tap connection, forcing agrarian/poor households to pool funds for shared taps, plus volumetric tariff hikes from NPR 20 to NPR 80 per 6,000 litres); (3) administrative rationing, moratoria on new tap applications (no new taps registered in Tansen since 1994; authorities refusing applications), and 11-year waiting queues in Bartung WUA alongside discretionary/corrupt queue-jumping for applicants paying double (NPR 100,000 / USD 880); and (4) registration rules requiring taps to be registered in male counterparts' names, barring women from association membership.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary mixed-methods empirical evidence from a 2016-17 survey of 350 households (142 in Tansen and 208 in Damauli), supplemented by focus group discussions and key informant discussions.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports multiple service-access outcomes at the household and municipal levels: access to municipal piped water supply (92.4% in Tansen vs 60.2% in Damauli), private vs shared tap connections, connection wait times (up to 11 years), supply duration and seasonal continuity, per capita consumption (41.42 lpcd in Tansen vs 65.9 lpcd in Damauli), affordability, and reliance on springs or private water tankers (with rented and peri-urban households excluded from tanker water by affordability constraints).
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and units of analysis (households and DWUAs/cooperatives in Tansen and Damauli municipalities, n = 350 surveyed households), exposure (DWUA/cooperative governance, regulatory autonomy, connection fees, application moratoria/queues, tariffs, and tap registration rules), outcomes, and study design (comparative mixed-methods case study).

evidence_quotes.quote: This paper focuses on the role of water user groups in providing access to drinking water in two urban locations in Nepal.
They are regulated by the Drinking Water Regulation 1998 which defines a water supplier as a WUA and/or licensee holding a licence for the operation of a water supply system.
In households of the Bartung committee, for example, application for a new tap connection (costing NPR 50,000 (USD 440)) requires a long wait time to get one

Women, who are solely responsible for collecting and managing water in most of the households, are barred from the associations, as the tap is generally registered in the name of their male counterpart.
Household level data were collected from 350 households across the two towns (208 in Damauli and 142 in Tansen).

Piped water supply from the municipality is available only to 60% of surveyed households in the core urban wards of Damauli with the duration of supply being around one and half hours in almost 63% of households (see Tables 3 and 4).

raw_response.exposure: Utility ownership, regulatory structure, and access rules of community-managed Drinking Water Users' Associations (DWUAs) and water cooperatives (autonomous statutory governance under the Drinking Water Regulation 1998 without municipal scrutiny, moratoria on new tap applications, NPR 50,000 connection fees without subsidies, 11-year waiting queues versus NPR 100,000 expedited connection payments, volumetric tariff increases, and male-counterpart tap registration rules)
raw_response.outcome: Household access to municipal piped drinking water and private vs shared tap connections, waiting time for connection, supply duration and seasonal continuity, per capita water consumption (lpcd), affordability, and coping reliance on springs or private tankers
raw_response.population_and_sample: Urban and peri-urban households and Drinking Water Users' Associations/cooperatives in Tansen and Damauli (Vyas) municipalities, Nepal; primary survey of 350 households (142 in Tansen and 208 in Damauli) plus focus group discussions and key informant interviews
raw_response.rationale: This comparative mixed-methods empirical study of 350 households and qualitative focus group discussions in two Nepalese municipalities (Tansen and Damauli) meets all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Beyond general operational management, it directly examines utility ownership and regulatory structure (statutory DWUAs/cooperatives operating autonomously without municipal oversight) alongside concrete rule-type access barriers: freezes on new tap applications, high upfront connection charges (NPR 50,000) without pro-poor subsidies forcing shared-tap pooling, 11-year connection queues bypassed by informal double payments (NPR 100,000), tariff increases, and male-name tap registration rules excluding women, linked to empirical outcomes on piped connection access, supply duration, continuity, consumption (lpcd), and affordability.
raw_response.study_design: Comparative mixed-methods case study (cross-sectional survey of 350 households combined with focus group discussions and key informant discussions)
